Expressing and Analyzing Quantum Algorithms with Qualtran

Matthew P. Harrigan Email: mpharrigan@google.com Thanks: Equal contribution Affiliation: Google Quantum AI, Venice, CA 90291, United States    Tanuj Khattar Email: tanujkhattar@google.com Thanks: Equal contribution Affiliation: Google Quantum AI, Venice, CA 90291, United States    Charles Yuan Affiliation: Google Quantum AI, Venice, CA 90291, United States Affiliation: MIT CSAIL, Cambridge, MA 02139, United States    Anurudh Peduri Affiliation: Google Quantum AI, Venice, CA 90291, United States Affiliation: Ruhr University Bochum, 44801 Bochum, Germany    Noureldin Yosri Affiliation: Google Quantum AI, Venice, CA 90291, United States    Fionn D. Abstract

Quantum computing’s transition from theory to reality has spurred the need for novel software tools to manage the increasing complexity, sophistication, toil, and fallibility of quantum algorithm development. We present Qualtran, an open-source library for representing and analyzing quantum algorithms. Using appropriate abstractions and data structures, we can simulate and test algorithms, automatically generate information-rich diagrams, and tabulate resource requirements. Qualtran offers a standard library of algorithmic building blocks that are essential for modern cost-minimizing compilations. Its capabilities are showcased through the re-analysis of key algorithms in Hamiltonian simulation, chemistry, and cryptography. Architecture-independent resource counts output by Qualtran can be forwarded to our implementation of cost models to estimate physical costs like wall-clock time and number of physical qubits assuming a surface-code architecture. Qualtran provides a foundation for explicit constructions and reproducible analysis, fostering greater collaboration within the growing quantum algorithm development community.

I Introduction

As quantum computing technology develops so too must our ability to leverage it for computational advantages. Luckily, we know of many applications for which quantum algorithms can give a meaningful asymptotic speedup relative to a classical computer [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]. The real-world computational advantage of a quantum algorithm, however, depends not only on its idealized asymptotic time complexity, but also on constants governed by algorithmic implementation and physical realities of quantum architectures such as error correction. Notably, the most competitive forms of quantum error correction known today incur large space-time overheads that can jeopardize advantage [6, 7]. Thus, accurately determining the advantage of a quantum algorithm running on hardware requires fully compiling the algorithm and determining its cost in terms of concrete constants. While resource estimation is not a new activity in quantum information [8] the scale and complexity of modern quantum algorithms demands improved tools for algorithm analysis and construction.

To analyze the constant factors of compiling a quantum algorithm to an error-corrected quantum computer, researchers typically record each operation using a mixture of enumerated lists and tables, mathematical Dirac notation, and English prose in a scientific journal article [9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16]. The challenge is that state-of-the-art quantum algorithms exist at the scale of teraquops — 101210^{12} qubits ×\times operations [17].

At that scale, a manual analysis is tedious, consuming months of researcher time and dozens of pages in a publication. For example, the manual resource analysis in Ref. [11] consumes Appendices A–D (16 pages), in Ref. [17] it consumes Appendices A–F (37 pages), and in Ref. [13] it consumes Appendix VII (41 pages). Such analysis is imprecise, requiring a researcher to approximate in an ad hoc way the cost of many operations lacking clear references from the literature. It is also inaccessible, yielding numerical figures that are hard for a reader to reproduce or extend.

Researchers have previously developed quantum programming languages, including Quipper [18], Scaffold [19], QWire [20], Q# [21], Silq [22], Tower [23], and Qrisp [24], that enable the programmer to express algorithms in a structured way that respects the abilities and constraints of a theoretical quantum computer. There are also existing frameworks for programming noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) computers at the circuit level within a Python host language such as Cirq [25], pyQuil [26], and Qiskit [27]. Taking inspiration from the useful features of existing languages, we contend that there is ample opportunity to experiment with new abstractions, tools, and ideas for quantum programming.

In this manuscript, we introduce Qualtran, an open-source, Python-based software framework that enables a researcher to express and analyze quantum algorithms for error-corrected quantum computers in an automated, precise, and accessible way. Qualtran offers a) data structures to represent quantum programs by hierarchically composing subroutines; b) methods to analyze the performance of quantum programs, including hardware resource costs; c) a library of re-usable algorithms and subroutines based on recent research on compilation and resource estimation; and d) a set of hardware architecture-aware models for estimating physical costs from architecture-agnostic costs.

We begin with a description of the design of the software tool—its data structures and analysis routines—in Section II. We then provide a survey of algorithmic primitives we consider essential for modern compilation studies in Section III. Next, Sections IV, V and VI demonstrate how Qualtran can be used on representative problems in quantum algorithms compilation including Hamiltonian simulation, ground state chemistry problems, and breaking cryptosystems. We describe the various physical cost models for translating the hardware-agnostic logical costs analyzed in the prior sections to physical quantities in Section VII, and conclude with closing remarks in Section VIII.

II Design of the Qualtran Framework

In designing the Qualtran framework, we adopted design principles that we believe distinguishes it from prior work. In particular, we have aimed to explicitly address the needs of practicing quantum algorithms researchers, who are already publishing studies on compiling large quantum algorithms—often without the use of any software tool. We specifically aim to accelerate this work rather than obviate it.

One principle is that the framework itself should be accessible and predictable. We motivate this by a contrast with classical programming languages: the C++ programming language has hundreds of developers contributing to the language infrastructure and millions of programmers agnostic to the particulars of the compilation infrastructure. Quantum algorithms research is not at this stage of maturity. Instead, researchers have to understand the problem domain, quantum algorithms, techniques for compiling quantum algorithms, and analysis techniques for reasoning about the cost and correctness of a program one cannot yet run. We designed Qualtran so that the runtime—in addition to the library of quantum algorithms—is readable, documented, extensible Python code. The software tries to be as predictable as possible: there is no special syntax, mutable state is avoided or carefully controlled, interfaces and types are explicit, and interoperability with the existing ecosystem of scientific computing Python packages is straightforward.

A second principle is that researchers need only annotate as much—or as little—about their algorithms and subroutines as is necessary to complete their research objectives. We seek meaningful statements about the correctness or cost of a quantum algorithm, not an executable ‘binary’ for a quantum program. When authoring a quantum subroutine, the user can either employ a placeholder with literature-based cost expressions or provide a full implementation of the subroutine. This flexibility is powerful: the system can emit a compiled circuit composed of logical 1- and 2-qubit gates if full implementations of each subroutine is provided. Alternatively, a user can quickly tabulate resource costs by outlining the expensive part of an algorithm.

The final principle is that the standard library of quantum algorithm primitives included in the framework should prioritize subroutines developed for—and used by—recent resource estimation studies. Section III provides additional detail for this principle, and highlights some of the most important primitives available in the standard library.

In the remainder of this section, we give an overview of the design of the Qualtran framework and how it enables a developer to express and analyze quantum algorithms. We first introduce the central data structures in Qualtran that enable a developer to build quantum programs in a modular way. We then present protocols for analyzing quantum programs in Qualtran, including gate counting, qubit counting, and simulation.

II.1 Bloqs: Building Blocks of Quantum Algorithms

To enable the developer to express quantum algorithms, Qualtran provides bloqs, which are data structures that represent quantum operations, subroutines, and programs. Some examples of bloqs include simple unitary quantum logic gates over individual qubits such as Hadamard, phase, and multi-controlled NOT\mathrm{NOT} gates; complex operations acting on registers of qubits such as multiplication, reflection, and state preparation; and select non-unitary operations including qubit allocation and deallocation.

We introduce a new term for this category of objects to avoid any implied constraints imposed by existing labels, and chose the name bloq to highlight these objects’ role as the building blocks of a quantum algorithm. A minimal bloq is characterized only by its name and signature—the names and dimensions of its input and output quantum registers. All other properties, such as its underlying sequence of logic gates or its numerical denotation as a tensor, are optional annotations on a bloq. This optionality enables a developer to implement only the properties of a bloq for the analysis they desire to perform. For example, annotating the approximate gate count for the most costly subroutine in an algorithm can be used for resource estimation. With additional detail, the framework enables compilation of a program down to an elementary gate set.

In contrast to classical programming languages and many quantum languages, Qualtran does not represent quantum programs as a sequence of textual keywords and identifiers. Instead, we adopt a model in which bloqs are represented explicitly as data structures within the Python host language. This model is common in NISQ programming frameworks [25, 26, 27], as well as machine learning frameworks such as TensorFlow [28]. This approach provides us access to a general-purpose programming language for analyzing, visualizing, and testing algorithms, and we believe this combination of a familiar host language with abstractions for quantum algorithmic building blocks is particularly accessible and useful for researchers in quantum algorithms.

II.1.1 Composition of Bloqs

In Qualtran, the user defines a bloq by its decomposition into simpler bloqs. Qualtran provides atomic bloqs, such as individual logic gates, that serve as the base case of this recursive strategy. For any bloq, its constituents composed to form a compute graph—a directed acyclic graph (DAG) whose edges, or wires, represent the flow of quantum data.

In Fig. 2, we illustrate the compute graph formed by composing modular multiplication bloqs to define a modular exponentiation bloq. We can observe the graph structure and trace the flow of quantum information from left to right. Each edge represents the flow of quantum data from the output of one bloq to the input of a subsequent bloq. A wire may represent one qubit or a larger (quantum) value with a particular quantum data type such as an unsigned integer encoded in multiple qubits. In the example, the Allocate bloq outputs a 2048-bit quantum integer to accumulate the results of the subsequent multiplications. A user that needs fine-grained manipulation of the encoded data can use the Split bloq to address individual qubits, as seen in the treatment of the exponent register. Each qubit in the exponent is used as a control for a corresponding multiplication operation.

These two features, hierarchical decomposition of bloqs and quantum data types, improve the classical runtime performance of the library. By incrementally lowering one level of the bloq hierarchy at a time, each decomposition step need only concern itself with tens or thousands of constituent bloqs. It does not need to fully unroll a bloq into e.g. all 10910^{9} gates that would be needed to represent the bloq as a single circuit. Additionally, the classical memory footprint of the Python object for the bloq in Fig. 2 would not increase if the bit-width of the arithmetic was increased from 2048 to 4096 bits, since the individual bits of a large quantum data type need not be explicitly represented.

This design also offers correctness guarantees. For example, the no-cloning [29] and no-deletion [30] theorems mandate that every piece of quantum data must be used exactly once in any physically realizable quantum computation. Qualtran enforces this correctness property automatically and transparently to the user via principles of linear logic developed in programming language research [20]. The mechanism is that, under the hood, the user does not manage the graph structure directly but rather invokes user-facing functions to manipulate the wire connection points. These functions raise a runtime error whenever a wire connection point is used twice, or is left unused without being marked as a bloq’s input or output.

Finally, Qualtran avoids a class of errors due to misidentifying qubits [31] by eschewing the concept of an implicit pool of qubits or qubit addresses as found in existing frameworks [25, 26, 27]. Allocations and de-allocations are explicit bloqs in the compute graph. Also, each register has a string name used during composition rather than relying on order or index alone.

II.1.2 Quantum Data Types

The elementary unit of quantum information is the qubit. We can use a collection of qubits to encode data with quantum data types—such as integers and real numbers up to a given precision. As introduced in the previous section, Qualtran offers first-class support for quantum data types. The signature of a bloq reports not only the arity and names of its inputs and outputs, but also its quantum data type. Bloqs can only be composed if their wires have matching data types. Each data type can be queried to determine how the data is encoded to and from (qu)bits. The number of qubits for a data type is crucial for use in resource estimation.

Whereas classical programming languages have a fixed collection of primitive types based on the machine architecture such as int32 or float64, the quantum data types in Qualtran enable the user to specify an arbitrary bit-width for a register. For example, the QInt(8) type specifies an 8-bit signed integer and the QFxp(6, 4) type specifies a 6-bit fixed-point number with 4 fractional bits. This flexibility is important for estimating resource requirements of quantum algorithms that we anticipate to be limited by qubit count, and where using a larger-than-necessary type for a known range of values is too wasteful for emerging hardware architectures.

Qualtran provides data types for unsigned integers, one’s and two’s complement signed integers, integers in Montgomery form [32], and fixed-point real numbers. The framework enables the user to define custom data types by implementing the appropriate interface. Additionally, it offers special support for fixed-size multidimensional arrays of quantum data. For example, a bloq that selects a register from mm input registers and swaps it into the first position can define its signature as one control register and an array of mm QInt registers.

Qualtran does not support quantum sum (union) or product (struct) types, and by extension does not support quantum strings or quantum lists [23]. This design accounts for the relative difficulty of estimating the resource costs of such data types under constraints of foreseeable quantum architectures, but may be revisited in future versions of the library.

II.2 Protocols for Analyzing Quantum Programs

We cannot yet execute the large-scale quantum algorithms expressed in Qualtran that require an error-corrected quantum computer. Nevertheless, researchers today labor to prototype, compile, and analyze quantum algorithms so that we may accurately predict the practical speedup of a given algorithm and obtain the most use out of an emerging hardware device. Qualtran aids researchers in this goal through protocols that act on quantum programs built from bloqs to query or derive useful properties, produce visualizations and diagrams, and check correctness of algorithms and subroutines.

II.2.1 Call Graphs

A basic task given a quantum program in bloq form is to compute and visualize the set of bloqs to which it decomposes, which in turn empowers downstream analyses such as gate and qubit counting. The data structure that Qualtran uses for this analysis is a call graph, a directed acyclic graph that has an edge pointing from a caller bloq to a callee bloq whenever the callee is in the collection of bloqs to which the caller decomposes. Each edge is annotated with the number of times the callee is called. Qualtran represents a call graph as a NetworkX [33] graph obtained by calling a designated method on a bloq.

A bloq can define its behavior and callees in two ways. The first way is to define a full decomposition that specifies the compute graph, including the explicit flow of information between the inputs and outputs of callees. In turn, Qualtran recovers a call graph from a compute graph by discarding detail and retaining only relationships between callers and callees. A full decomposition is needed for tasks such as simulation, but is not always required to accomplish a researcher’s goals when considering the effort.

As an alternative, the bloq may define a call graph decomposition that simply lists the callees (and their number of calls) without accounting for the flow of quantum information. This approach is sufficient for certain analyses, such as gate counts, and has three advantages over full decomposition:

  • •

    The user can quickly estimate costs by only providing the unstructured list of callees.

  • •

    Parameters can propagate as symbolic rather than concrete values. For example, consider a bloq that applies the XX gate on a parametric number of qubits nn. Its full decomposition would instantiate nn XGate objects, and the Python runtime cannot instantiate a symbolic number of objects. By contrast, the call graph decomposition simply states that the bloq uses n​Xn\ X gates, where nn is a SymPy [34] variable that supports arithmetic.

  • •

    The call graph decomposition can serve as an automated cross-check of correctness against a full decomposition of the bloq if the user provides both.

Given a bloq, we can visualize its compute and call graphs in order to validate constructions and communicate algorithms. Qualtran supports drawing these graphs, complete with annotations on each bloq such as qubit and gate counts. The framework can draw the compute graph of a bloq either as a directed acyclic graph as in Figure 2 via Graphviz [35], or as a traditional quantum circuit via ⟨𝗊|𝗉𝗂𝖼⟩\bra{\mathsf{q}}\ket{\mathsf{pic}} [36].11 1 In Qualtran, we term this style a musical score diagram for disambiguation from other references to circuits.

II.2.2 Gate Counting

The first essential question about a quantum algorithm is how many operations must be performed to execute the algorithm. Although the associated physical wall-clock time will depend on details of the target hardware architecture and error-correcting code (see Section VII), the quantity and type of quantum logic gates serves as a useful architecture-independent proxy for the time cost of an algorithm.

Qualtran enables a researcher to automatically count the number of gates comprising a quantum algorithm. For an algorithm expressed as a bloq, the system recursively sums the contributions from the callees to which the bloq decomposes. This analysis is simple and is not fundamentally tied to any particular target architecture. The analysis is also efficient: by automatically caching the computed costs of reoccurring bloqs, Qualtran can compute gate counts for algorithms containing hundreds of millions of gates in a matter of seconds.

There are two specific strategies included for gate counting. The BloqCounts strategy requires researchers to explicitly specify the bloqs they wish to count, but affords the user complete control over the target gateset or architecture. In contemporary literature on quantum resource estimation, however, researchers often map an algorithm onto a quantum architecture that uses the surface code for error correction. To account for gate costs, researchers typically count TT and Toffoli gates, the quantity (but not specific identity) of Clifford gates, arbitrary-angle rotation gates, and measurement operations [37, 38, 39]. The QECGatesCost strategy that is pre-configured to count the gates most relevant to a surface code error corrected architecture.

In designing this second strategy, it became apparent that there is no strict agreement in the literature on specifically which fault tolerant gates to count and when to ‘stop’ decomposing. Some studies will continue compiling an algorithm until only Clifford and TT gates remain; while others will count other basic gates like the Toffoli or Fredkin gate independently of the TT count. Indeed, there are some surface code architectures that have different costs for directly implementing Toffoli gates compared to compiling them to four or seven TT gates. In our design of the QECGatesCost gate counting routine, we keep the counts factored by their gate type as much as possible and provide methods to aggregate counts for a particular choice of gate set.

The gate counts can be insightful in their own right by comparing the runtime costs of algorithms in an architecture-independent way, or they can be fed into the physical cost models detailed in Section VII.

II.2.3 Qubit Counting

The second essential property of a quantum algorithm is how many qubits it requires. While the number of required physical qubits will also depend on the target hardware architecture (see Section VII), the number of logical, error-corrected qubits is architecture-independent. Using Qualtran, a researcher can automatically estimate the number of logical qubits required by a quantum algorithm.

Qualtran counts qubits in a hierarchical and recursive way. It assumes that each callee in the decomposition of a bloq executes sequentially, and computes the number of qubits at each sequence point as the number of qubits required by the callee plus the number of idle qubits acting as bystanders. In assuming that callees execute sequentially, Qualtran minimizes qubit count potentially at the expense of greater circuit depth or execution time. Conversely, by assuming that each callee uses all of its qubits for its entire execution, Qualtran potentially overestimates the qubit count. We believe that this Min-Max-style estimate can provide a good balance between accuracy and scalability of the accounting.

We discuss two important considerations for designing a qubit counting algorithm: First, bloqs can allocate and free qubits within their decomposition; so we cannot simply look at the input and output sizes of a bloq to determine its qubit cost. Second, the qubit count cannot be expressed as the maximum over the qubit counts of all the callees: when executing a particular callee, the number of qubits is at least the number of qubits required by the callee plus the number of idle, bystander qubits that are output or inputs to other callees.

There are optimizations that are only possible by fully decomposing a bloq to a circuit by flattening hierarchical structure and carefully tessellating operations from different components. Such strategies are employed for circuits of thousands of gates that run on current generation, NISQ hardware. Indeed, one can use the interoperability features of Qualtran to convert a program to a Cirq circuit with such optimizations, but this is likely not feasible for large-scale algorithms with billions of gates. It is a future direction to investigate more accurate qubit allocations without sacrificing tractability.

Overall, Qualtran makes simplifying assumptions by default that efficiently estimate the number of qubits used by many quantum algorithms, and we have designed the the framework to be sufficiently general that a developer can write their own routine for counting qubits if additional precision is necessary.

II.2.4 Tensor Simulation

In the absence of a hardware quantum computer, researchers often check whether a quantum program is correct by simulating it on a classical computer. In general, such simulation requires an exponential amount of classical resources. A state vector simulation stores 2n2^{n} complex numbers to simulate an nn-qubit system, while a Feynman path integral simulation uses constant space but exponential time to sum over an exponential number of paths [40]. Thus, simulation is tractable only for bloqs that use few qubits or exhibit special structure. Nevertheless, by testing the numerical simulation of small instances of a bloq, we gain confidence that the implementation is correct at problem-relevant scales as well.

Qualtran can simulate a quantum program by deriving its state vector or unitary (its tensor) from the tensors of its constituent bloqs. We use the tensor network techniques provided by Quimb [41] to find good tensor contraction orderings—which interpolate between the state vector and Feynman path approaches—that decrease the cost of simulating complex bloqs. As an example, we have successfully used Qualtran to test that a 32-bit quantum adder circuit consisting of 64 qubits works correctly on given input/output states via a simulation that uses only 6 qubits’ worth of classical memory.

II.2.5 Classical Simulation

Whereas full tensor simulation has exponentially large cost in general, many common quantum algorithmic primitives merely perform classical reversible logic on data that just happens to exist in superposition. We can efficiently simulate such operations as part of testing a complex algorithm on classical inputs and outputs. For example, the quantum lookup table primitive of Section III.3 has semantics identical to a table lookup on a classical computer, except that the index register contains a superposition of indices so that the operation loads a superposition of the classical data at each index.

Qualtran has explicit support for simulating and testing bloqs that encode classical logic as above. First, a bloq author annotates how the bloq acts over classical data by providing corresponding Python code. Qualtran uses this logic to propagate classical values through bloqs and produce a classical output. Then, the user can perform an analogue to fuzz testing in classical software engineering by sampling a set of classical input/output pairs and comparing to the outputs of the classical simulation. After testing enough pairs of classical values, the user can gain confidence that the quantum construction is correct.

III Essential Quantum Subroutines in the Qualtran Standard Library

In this section, we present a core set of subroutines and techniques to manipulate quantum information that underpin the diverse world of quantum algorithms. These techniques are not traditionally taught as part of quantum information classes, nor do they appear in standard quantum computing textbooks. Instead, they emerge from quantum resource estimation studies from the last decade, painstakingly derived again and again in the prose of paper appendices. By collecting these subroutines in the Qualtran standard library, we aim to bring these essential tools to the forefront and empower researchers to quickly express quantum algorithms at a high level of abstraction without sacrificing the latest advancements in performance engineering. However, we view this library as merely the beginning, not the end. Our aspiration is to vastly expand it over time as we continue our work on resource estimation. We also hope that the open source community will actively contribute to building more primitives for the standard library, fostering a collaborative effort to enrich this vital resource for quantum algorithm development.

In each of the following sections, we highlight the quantum algorithmic primitive as a bloq or set of bloqs and demonstrate its construction through code snippets along with error propagation and visualization:

  • •

    In Section III.1, we describe Qualtran’s features for performing rotations of quantum states that are used by modern fault-tolerant algorithms. Supported rotations include direct synthesis, phase kickback on a Fourier state, and probabilistic implementations using generalized state injection.

  • •

    In Section III.2, we describe Qualtran’s features for selecting quantum operations via a quantum index using iterator circuits that can be reused in a wide variety of tasks. Specifically, in Section III.3, we show how this tool can be used to load classical data into quantum superposition.

  • •

    In Section III.4, we describe Qualtran’s features for preparing arbitrary quantum states and arbitrary purified density matrices. We describe the context in which these two state preparation tasks are useful and highlight the strategies supported by Qualtran for dense and sparse versions of these tasks.

  • •

    In Section III.5, we describe Qualtran’s block encoding library, which enables quantum algorithms to load datasets or transformations of states as matrices and to perform arithmetic operations such as tensor products, products, and linear combinations on the encoded matrices.

  • •

    In Section III.6, we describe Qualtran’s support for quantum signal processing, which enable algorithms to transform block encodings via arbitrary polynomials.

  • •

    Finally, in Section III.7, we present bloq constructions of modern phase estimation techniques using window functions.

III.1 Rotations

Rotations are a fundamental class of operations in quantum algorithms with substantial space/time cost differences depending on their implementation. The selection of an optimal strategy to perform arbitrary rotations can depend on algorithmic context and hardware context—i.e. limiting regimes such as early fault-tolerant quantum computers with few logical qubits. Thus, Qualtran provides a number of ways to achieve arbitrary rotations to varying precision with different quantum resource overheads. While we do not support program analysis to automatically choose the optimal rotation primitive, many bloqs in Qualtran default to one of the following strategies which make the most algorithmic sense.

The lowest level rotation primitives supported by Qualtran are single-qubit ZZ-axis rotations. We consider two standard conventions defining the rotation, RzR_{z} and ZPow\ZPow,

Rz(θ)=e−iZθ/2=(e−iθ/200ei​θ/2),ZPow(t)=(100ei​π​t)=ei​π​t/2Rz(πt)R_{z}(\theta)=e^{-iZ\theta/2}=\begin{pmatrix}e^{-i\theta/2}&0\\ 0&e^{i\theta/2}\end{pmatrix}\;\;,\;\;\ZPow(t)=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\ 0&e^{i\pi t}\end{pmatrix}=e^{i\pi t/2}R_{z}(\pi t)

which are equivalent up to global phase. The parameterization of each gate has different domains; RzR_{z} angle θ∈[0,2​π)\theta\in[0,2\pi) satisfying Rz​(π)=−i​ZR_{z}(\pi)=-iZ, and for ZPow\ZPow t∈[0,2)t\in[0,2), satisfying ZPow⁡(1)=Z\ZPow(1)=Z. At the time of publication, the Qualtran standard library supports three techniques to achieve these rotations which are described in Table 1 along with their resource costs.

For arbitrary axis single-qubit rotations, Qualtran provides the SU2RotationGate which accepts any 2×22\times 2 unitary matrix and a precision ϵ\epsilon, and decomposes into three ZZ rotations each with precision ϵ/3\epsilon/3. Controlled variants of all single-qubit rotations (ZZ-axis and arbitrary axis) are also supported using circuit identities which reduce controlled Z rotations to uncontrolled Z rotations [43, 45].

The Qualtran standard library also provides support for a broad class of generalized basis state phasing through the Quantum Variable Rotation (QVR) [43, 11] set of bloqs. Two examples are, optimized versions of Hamming weight phasing [46] and phasing by an arbitrary cost functions used in recent resource estimation studies of combinatorial optimization [11].

III.1.1 Single Qubit Z Rotation

Here we expand on the single qubit ZZ-axis rotations described in Table 1 and provide an example invocation code block.

Direct Clifford+T Synthesis.

Bocharov et al. [42] synthesized ZZ rotations by the use of repeat-until-success circuits which have an expected T-gate cost of

⌈1.149​log⁡1ϵ+9.2⌉.\left\lceil 1.149\log\frac{1}{\epsilon}+9.2\right\rceil. (1)

The bloqs ZPow and Rz accept a precision ϵ\epsilon, and rotation exponent/angle (tt, θ\theta respectively). The rotation angle and precision inputs can be invoked as symbolic values or numerical values.

Programmable Ancilla Rotations.

Originally presented in Jones et al. [43, Sec. 2.3], this technique performs ZZ rotations using state-injection into a repeat-until-success circuit. Such techniques are often useful in situations where expensive resource states can be prepared ahead of time (possibly in parallel), reducing overhead during the run of the algorithm. To synthesize an ZPow⁡(t)\ZPow(t), this method uses a set of pre-prepared resource states |ω(k)⟩\ket{\omega^{(k)}}, called programmed ancillas, defined as

|ω(k)⟩=ZPow⁡(2k​t)​|+⟩=12​(|0⟩+e2k​i​π​t​|1⟩).\displaystyle\ket{\omega^{(k)}}=\ZPow(2^{k}t)\ket{+}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\left\lparen\ket{0}+e^{2^{k}i\pi t}\ket{1}\right\rparen. (2)

The bloq’s instantiation requires three parameters: exponent tt, precision ϵ\epsilon, and the expected number of rounds nn which defaults to 2. The total rotation cost is computed by adding costs to synthesize nn resource ancilla in state |ω(k)⟩\ket{\omega^{(k)}}, each with precision ϵ/n\epsilon/n.

Rotation by addition into a phase-gradient state.

Rotations can be performed by phase kickback when adding a value into a phase-gradient state [47, 11, 46]. The phase-gradient state is a Fourier state defined over bgradb_{\mathrm{grad}} qubits

|ϕgrad⟩=12bgrad∑k=02bgrad−1e−2πik/2bgrad|k2bgrad⟩=⨂j=1bgrad|0⟩+e−2πik/2j|1⟩2\ket{\phi_\text{grad}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2^{b_{\text{grad}}}}}\sum_{k=0}^{2^{b_{\text{grad}}}-1}e^{-2\pi ik/2^{b_{\text{grad}}}}\ket{\frac{k}{2^\bgrad}}=\bigotimes_{j=1}^{{b_{\text{grad}}}}\frac{\ket{0}+e^{-2\pi ik/2^{j}}\ket{1}}{\sqrt{2}} (3)

where bgradb_{\mathrm{grad}} sets the precision for the rotation. Qualtran supports construction of this state using the bloq PhaseGradientState which can be used as an input wire for the rotation. The phase gradient state |ϕgrad⟩\ket{\phi_\text{grad}} is catalytic in the sense that it can be reused for multiple rotations.

The rotation bloq ZPowConstViaPhaseGradient accepts an exponent tt and the phase-gradient size bgrad{b_{\text{grad}}}, and implements a ZPow⁡(t)\ZPow(t). We provide a utility function ZPowConstViaPhaseGradient.from_precision to allow the user to construct the rotation from precision requirements, shown in Fig. 3.

III.1.2 Quantum Variable Rotation

A Quantum Variable Rotation (QVR) [43, 11] is a unitary which phases each computational basis state |x⟩|x\rangle by e2​π​i​xe^{2\pi ix}. QVR has been used as a primitive for quantum chemistry simulations [43] and combinatorial optimization [11]. An nn-qubit QVR unitary can be defined as

QVR⁡∑j=02n−1n⁡cj​|xj⟩↦∑j=02n−1e2​π​i​xj​cj​|xj⟩\QVR_{n}\sum_{j=0}^{2^{n}-1}c_{j}\ket{x_j}\mapsto\sum_{j=0}^{2^{n}-1}e^{2\pi ix_{j}}c_{j}\ket{x_j}

Here, the basis xj∈[0,1)x_{j}\in[0,1) are interpreted as nn-bit fractional values. In general, we implement an approximate QVR\QVR, denoted by QVRn,ϵ\QVR_{n,\epsilon}, which is ϵ\epsilon-close to the above unitary by the distance measure from Ref. [44, Eq. 1].

Qualtran provides two bloqs to perform QVR. The first is QvrZPow, which accepts an integer nn and a precision ϵ\epsilon, and implements QVRn,ϵ\QVR_{n,\epsilon} by decomposing into nn single qubit ZPow\ZPow rotations applied to the nn-bit input register, each with accuracy ϵn\frac{\epsilon}{n} [43, Fig. 14]. Each single qubit ZZ rotation can be synthesized using any of the techniques in Section III.1.1.

The second bloq for QVR is QvrPhaseGradient, which uses a quantum-quantum addition [46, 48] into a phase-gradient state (Eq. 3) to obtain a phase kickback on the input register. The constructor QvrPhaseGradient.from_bitsize accepts an integer nn and a precision ϵ\epsilon and implements QVRn,ϵ\QVR_{n,\epsilon}.

For ease of exposition, we considered a simplified definition of QVR above. Qualtran also implements bloqs for more general definitions of QVR [43, 11] which have a constant γ\gamma programmed into them, and phase by a value e2​π​i​γ​xe^{2\pi i\gamma x}. It also provides PhasingViaCostFunction, which accepts a bloq computing function f⁡(x)f(x) and phases by e2​π​i​f​(x)e^{2\pi if(x)} [11]. For example, the HammingWeightPhasing bloq uses hamming weight as the cost function, to apply parallel ZPow⁡(t)\ZPow(t) gates to nn qubits more efficiently [46].

III.2 Unary Iteration and Indexed Operations

The unary iteration primitive is a quantum analogue of a classical for-loop. Specifically, we wish to construct a unitary operation UU that acts on a selection register of size SS and a target register of size TT; and its action is described as

U=∑i=0L−1|i⟩​⟨i|⊗ViU=\sum_{i=0}^{L-1}\ket{i}\bra{i}\otimes V_{i} (4)

where L=2SL=2^{S} is the number of unitaries ViV_{i} to apply on different branches of the superposition. This is the equivalent of a classical for-loop with a conditional as follows:

⬇
for ii in range(LL):
if ​s​e​l​e​c​t​i​o​n\emph{selection} register SS stores integer ii:
Apply ViV_{i} on ​t​a​r​g​e​t\emph{target} register TT

This primitive has been extensively used in the quantum algorithms literature, albeit by different names. Shende et al. [49] introduced this primitive as a Quantum Multiplexor and used it to develop a theory of quantum conditionals and to generalize several known constructions from digital logic, such as Shannon decomposition of Boolean functions. Childs et al. [50] introduced this primitive as the Select(V) operation and described an implementation via a tree traversal of a balanced binary tree with L=2SL=2^{S} leaf nodes using 1.5​L−11.5L-1 Toffoli gates and SS clean ancilla qubits. Babbush et al. [9] improved this construction to use L−1L-1 Toffoli gates using SS clean ancilla qubits and coined the term Unary Iteration. Sanders et al. [11] describes an optimization for iterating over a sparse set of indices with a Toffoli count that scales as min⁡(2S−1,S×|L|)\min(2^{S}-1,S\times\absolutevalue{L}) where |L|\absolutevalue{L} is the number of indices to iterate upon (i.e. the sparsity), SS is still the size of the selection register and now |L|\absolutevalue{L} can be ≪2S\ll 2^{S}. Khattar and Gidney [51] extends the construction of [9, 50] to use skew trees instead of balanced binary trees with either SS dirty ancilla qubits and cost 1.25​L+𝒪⁡(L)1.25L+\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{L}) Toffoli or log2∗​S\log_{2}^{*}{S} clean ancilla with 2.25​L2.25L Toffoli.

In Qualtran, the simplest API to use the unary iteration construction from Ref. [9] is via the ApplyLthBloq class. Given a list of bloqs=[V0,V1,…,VL−1]\text{bloqs}=[V_{0},V_{1},...,V_{L-1}] that all act on the same target registers, we can construct a bloq U = ApplyLthBloq(bloqs) such that

U=∑ℓ=0L−1|ℓ⟩​⟨ℓ|⊗VℓU=\sum_{\ell=0}^{L-1}\ket{\ell}\bra{\ell}\otimes V_{\ell}

The ApplyLthBloq class also supports specifying an NN-dimensional NumPy [52] array of subbloqs, in which case the bloq allocates NN selection registers, one for each dimension, and is equivalent to NN nested for-loops. Figure 4(a) shows how one can use the ApplyLthBloq to load 1D data in a target register and perform classical simulation to verify the decomposition is correct—i.e. the ii-th data element is loaded in the target register when the selection register stores integer ii. Figure 4(b) shows how the construction can be modified to load 2D data using two selection registers.

The ApplyLthBloq implements the interface defined by the abstract base class UnaryIterationGate, which can be used directly by power users who need more control on the tree iteration strategy when constructing the unary iteration circuit. For example, one can implement the “variable-spaced QROM” optimization presented in [11] by overriding the .break_early method to return ​T​r​u​e\emph{True} whenever all elements in the subtree are identical. Note that this example is purely for illustration and Qualtran provides native bloqs for loading classical data via QROM as described in Section III.3

III.3 Quantum Lookup Table: Encoding Classical Data as Basis States

Similar to a classical lookup table that returns classical data xix_{i} for a queried index ii, a quantum lookup table can be defined as a unitary OxO_{x} that responds with a superposition of classical data when queried with an arbitrary superposition of address bits ∑iαi​|i⟩\sum_{i}\alpha_{i}\ket{i}

Ox​∑i=0N−1αi​|i⟩​|0⟩→∑i=0N−1αi​|i⟩​|xi⟩O_{x}\sum_{i=0}^{N-1}\alpha_{i}\ket{i}\ket{0}\rightarrow\sum_{i=0}^{N-1}\alpha_{i}\ket{i}\ket{x_{i}} (5)

A variety of implementations [53, 9, 54] have been proposed in the literature for the quantum lookup table oracle defined in Equation 5. We refer the readers to Table I of Zhu et al. [55] for tradeoffs between the different proposals. In Qualtran, we provide built in Bloqs for some of the most commonly used implementations of a Quantum Lookup Table:

The QROM bloq implements the construction from Section III.C of Ref. [9], which is based on using the unary iteration construction described in Equation 4, and also implements the variable-spaced QROM optimization from Figure 3 of Ref. [11] which reduces gate counts when the data to be loaded is sparse in terms of number of unique elements.

The SelectSwapQROM bloq implements the construction from Figure 1d of Low et al. [54], which uses 𝒪⁡(N)\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{N}) additional ancillas to reduce the T / Toffoli gate count by a factor of 𝒪⁡(N)~\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{N}). In this construction, a configurable parameter K=2kK=2^{k} is chosen and b⋅Kb\cdot K dirty ancilla qubits are used as targets to load a N/KN/K batches of data, each of size KK. The Toffoli cost of the resulting construction is 2​⌈N/K⌉+4​b​(K−1)2\lceil N/K\rceil+4b(K-1).

The QROAMClean bloq implements the optimized variant of SelectSwapQROM described in Appendix  A, B of Berry et al. [56], which assumes the target register is always initialized in the |0⟩\ket{0} state. In this construction, b⋅(K−1)b\cdot(K-1) clean ancilla qubits are used as targets to load the batched data, and measurement based uncomputation is used to clean up the clean ancilla registers. The Toffoli cost of the resulting construction ⌈N/K⌉+b⁡(K−1)\lceil N/K\rceil+b(K-1).

The QROAMCleanAdjoint bloq implements measurement based uncomputation of a table lookup via the construction described Appendix C of Berry et al. [56], which assumes the target register should be left in the |0⟩\ket{0} state after uncomputation. This construction reduces a table lookup over NN elements, each of target bitsize bb to a table lookup of N/2N/2 elements, each of target bitsize 22, by first measuring the target register in the X-basis and using the measurement outcomes to do a corrective table lookup. The corrective table lookup is applied using a construction similar to QROAMClean. Thus, the Toffoli cost of the resulting construction is ⌈N/K⌉+K\lceil N/K\rceil+K.

All of the bloqs for quantum table lookup described above support loading multiple classical datasets, where each dataset can be multi-dimensional. For SelectSwapQROM and its variants, the bloq implementation incorporates optimizations to choose multiple block sizes, one for each dimension of the classical dataset, as described in Appendix G of Lee et al. [17]

III.4 Quantum State Preparation: Encoding Classical Data as Amplitudes

Quantum State Preparation is the task to encode an NN-dimensional vector of classical data a→=(a0,a1,…,aN−1)\vec{a}=(a_{0},a_{1},\dots,a_{N-1}) as amplitudes of NN computational basis states over n=log⁡(N)n=\log{N} qubits. The problem has been widely studied in the quantum algorithms literature [57, 58, 49, 59, 54, 60] and has applications across quantum chemistry [9, 56, 61, 62, 63], quantum dynamics [10, 64], and solving systems of linear equations [65, 66].

In this section, we describe two variants of the quantum state preparation problem, both of which assume that classical data to be encoded is given as entries of a classical database and no specific structure about the data is assumed. For both the variants described below, a sparse version of the problem can be defined analogously where the number of non-zero entries in the classical description of the state is specified by a sparsity parameter S≪NS\ll N. Note that when specific structure about the state to be prepared is known, one can often [67, 60] do better than the arbitrary state preparation routines discussed below. For example, PrepareUniformSuperposition bloq in Qualtran can be used to prepare a uniform superposition over the first NN basis states, where NN may not be a power of 2, using a single round of amplitude amplification as described in Babbush et al. [9].

III.4.1 Preparation of Arbitrary Quantum States

The arbitrary quantum state preparation problem seeks to encode classical data described by an NN dimensional vector of complex numbers a→=(a0,a1,…,aN−1)\vec{a}=(a_{0},a_{1},\dots,a_{N-1}), such that ax=|ax|​ei​ϕ​(x)a_{x}=\absolutevalue{a_x}e^{i\phi(x)}, as amplitudes of a quantum state with NN basis vectors prepared on n=log2​Nn=\log_{2}{N} qubits such that the prepared state |ψ⟩prep\ket{\psi}_{\text{prep}} is ϵ\epsilon-close to the desired state |ψ⟩f\ket{\psi}_{f} defined as

|ψ⟩f=1‖a→‖2​∑x=0N−1ax​|x⟩\ket{\psi}_{f}=\frac{1}{\norm{\Vec{a}}_{2}}\sum_{x=0}^{N-1}a_{x}\ket{x} (6)

where ‖a→‖2=∑x|ax|2\norm{\Vec{a}}_{2}=\sqrt{\sum_{x}\absolutevalue{a_x}^{2}} is a normalization constant and

‖|ψ⟩prep−|ψ⟩f‖2≤ϵ\norm{\ket{\psi}_\text{prep} - \ket{\psi}_{f}}_{2}\leq\epsilon

where ‖.‖2\norm{.}_{2} is the Euclidean norm.

In Qualtran, the StatePreparationViaRotations bloq implements the technique for arbitrary state preparation described in Low et al. [54], which reduces state preparation over nn qubits and N=2nN=2^{n} elements to nn data lookups of length [1,2,4,…,2n−1][1,2,4,\dots,2^{n-1}] elements, each loading a bb-bit approximation of a rotation angle. Each data lookup is followed by bb single-qubit controlled rotations. Thus, a total of N=1+2+⋯+2n−1N=1+2+\dots+2^{n-1} data elements are loaded, each of bitsize bb, across nn different lookup calls and 𝒪⁡(n×b)\mathcal{O}(n\times b) single qubit controlled rotations are applied. Each data lookup step is implemented via techniques described in Section III.3 and the single qubit rotations are synthesized via techniques described in Section III.1. Here b=log2⁡(n/ϵ)b=\log_{2}({n/\epsilon}) is chosen such that the prepared state is ϵ\epsilon-close to the desired state. The nn data lookups to load N=2nN=2^{n} rotation angles, each of size b=log2⁡(n/ϵ)b=\log_{2}({n/\epsilon}), dominate the overall cost of the algorithm.

For sparse state preparation, SparseStatePreparationViaRotations can be used which reduces sparse state preparation to dense state preparation via techniques described in Ramacciotti et al. [68].

III.4.2 Preparation of Arbitrary Purified Density Matrices

Arbitrary purified density matrix preparation seeks to encode classical data described by an NN-dimensional vector of positive real numbers w→=(w0,w1,…,wN−1)\vec{w}=(w_{0},w_{1},\dots,w_{N-1}), such that wi≥0∧wi∈ℛw_{i}\geq 0\land w_{i}\in\mathcal{R}, as probabilities of an ensemble of NN basis states represented by a density matrix ρprep\rho_{\text{prep}} which is ϵ\epsilon-close to the desired density matrix ρf\rho_{f} defined as

ρf=∑x=0N−1wx‖w→‖1​|x⟩​⟨x|\rho_{f}=\sum_{x=0}^{N-1}\frac{w_{x}}{\norm{\Vec{w}}_{1}}\ket{x}\bra{x} (7)

where ‖w→‖1=∑xwx\norm{\Vec{w}}_{1}=\sum_{x}w_{x} is a normalization constant and

‖ρprep−ρf‖1≤ϵ\norm{\rho_\text{prep} - \rho_f}_{1}\leq\epsilon

where ‖.‖1\norm{.}_{1} is the trace distance. This is achieved by preparing a purification of ρprep\rho_{\text{prep}} of the form

|ψ⟩prep=wx~‖w‖1​|x⟩​|tempx⟩\ket{\psi}_{\text{prep}}=\sqrt{\frac{\widetilde{w_{x}}}{\norm{w}_{1}}}\ket{x}\ket{\text{temp}_{x}} (8)

where the desired number state |x⟩\ket{x} is allowed to be entangled with a garbage state |tempx⟩\ket{\text{temp}_{x}} that depends only on xx. Such a state is often cheaper to prepare than preparation of arbitrary quantum states described in the previous section, and is sufficient for applications like quantum simulation based on linear combination of unitaries or qubitization [9, 61, 69].

In Qualtran, the StatePreparationAliasSampling bloq implements the technique for arbitrary purified density matrix preparation described in Babbush et al. [9], which reduces the problem of state preparation over n+μn+\mu qubits and N=2nN=2^{n} elements to that of a single data lookup to load NN elements, each of bitsize n+μn+\mu, followed by a quantum-quantum comparison and conditional swap. Here μ=⌈log2​1/ϵ⌉\mu=\lceil\log_{2}{1/\epsilon}\rceil is chosen such that the prepared state is ϵ\epsilon-close to the desired state. The data lookup step dominates the overall cost and is implemented via techniques described in Section III.3

For sparse state preparation, SparseStatePreparationAliasSampling can be used which reduces sparse state preparation to dense state preparation via techniques described in Section 5 of Berry et al. [56].

III.5 Block Encoding

Numerous quantum algorithms, including those for Hamiltonian simulation [17, 13], linear algebra [65, 70], and portfolio optimization [71], rely on loading a matrix of data or transforming a quantum state via a matrix. To do so, they utilize block encoding — a way to represent a matrix as a unitary operator when the matrix is not unitary, or is inconvenient or inefficient to directly realize as a unitary operator.

Let AA be an ss-qubit linear operator, which is not necessarily unitary. Following Ref. [72], we say that the (s+a)(s+a)-qubit unitary ℬ⁡[A]\mathcal{B}[A] is a (α,a,ϵ)(\alpha,a,\epsilon)-block encoding of AA if:

‖A−α⁡(⟨0|⊗a⊗I)​ℬ​[A]​(|0⟩⊗a⊗I)‖≤ϵ\norm{A - \alpha(\bra{0}^{\otimes a} \otimes I) \mathcal{B}[A] (\ket{0}^{\otimes a} \otimes I)}\leq\epsilon

where α\alpha is a normalization constant chosen such that ‖A‖/α≤1\norm{A}/\alpha\leq 1, and ϵ≥0\epsilon\geq 0 is the precision of the encoding. In other words, the matrix ℬ⁡[A]\mathcal{B}[A] contains A/αA/\alpha in its upper-left block:

ℬ⁡[A]=(A/α∗∗∗)\mathcal{B}[A]=\begin{pmatrix}A/\alpha&*\\ *&*\end{pmatrix}

Historically, the concept of block encoding emerged from methods to encode matrices as the input to algorithms for quantum linear algebra [65] and from methods to encode Hamiltonians as a linear combination of unitaries [63]. It gained prominence with the development of quantum recommendation systems [73] and optimal Hamiltonian simulation by qubitization [61]. It cemented its role at the forefront of interest in algorithms research with the development of the quantum singular value transformation [72].

Qualtran implements techniques to block-encode various matrices important to quantum algorithms. First, it provides bloqs to construct block encodings from primitive elements such as unitaries, LCU SELECT/PREPARE oracles, and sparse access matrices. Next, it provides bloqs to compose these block encodings by arithmetic operations such as products and linear combinations of the encoded matrices.

III.5.1 Primitive Block Encodings from Unitaries and Oracles

First, in the simplest case, any unitary operator UU is a (1,0,0)(1,0,0)-block encoding of UU. Correspondingly, the Unitary bloq in Qualtran wraps a unitary bloq into a block encoding with α=1\alpha=1.

Second, any linear combination of unitaries A=∑iλi​AiA=\sum_{i}\lambda_{i}A_{i} as specified by a pair of SELECT and PREPARE oracles defines a block encoding of AA, which can be created by Qualtran’s LCUBlockEncoding bloq.

Third, Qualtran’s SparseMatrix bloq constructs a block encoding for a sparse matrix AA with at most mm non-zero entries in each row or column, given oracles

Or​|i⟩​|k⟩=|i⟩​|ri​k⟩\displaystyle O_{r}\ket{i}\ket{k}=\ket{i}\ket{r_{ik}}
Oc​|j⟩​|ℓ⟩=|cj​ℓ⟩​|ℓ⟩\displaystyle O_{c}\ket{j}\ket{\ell}=\ket{c_{j\ell}}\ket{\ell}

to compute the index ri​jr_{ij} or cj​ic_{ji} of the jj-th nonzero entry in the ii-th row or column respectively of AA, and

OA​|i⟩​|j⟩​|0⟩=|i⟩​|j⟩​|Ai​j⟩O_{A}\ket{i}\ket{j}\ket{0}=\ket{i}\ket{j}\ket{A_{ij}}

to compute the matrix entry Ai​jA_{ij} [71].

Qualtran provides a set of pre-implemented row/column oracles for matrices where the non-zero elements are located in the top-left block (TopLeftRowColumnOracle) or within a band along the main diagonal (SymmetricBandedRowColumnOracle). It also provides pre-implemented entry oracles for matrices where all elements have equal value (UniformEntryOracle) or are explicitly given by a NumPy array that is loaded from QROM (ExplicitEntryOracle). In the more general case, Qualtran gives interfaces and subroutines to aid the user in implementing a custom oracle.

Dense matrices can be encoded as a special case of sparse matrices. In Fig. 6(a), we present an example of the encoding of a dense 2×22\times 2 matrix explicitly given as a NumPy array. The example uses TopLeftRowColumnOracle to specify that the top left 21×212^{1}\times 2^{1} block, i.e. the entire matrix, is nonzero. It uses ExplicitEntryOracle to specify the entries to be loaded from QROM. Though this example block encoding incurs larger costs than a sparse matrix given by a more efficient entry access oracle, it shows how a developer can quickly prototype the loading of a dataset or transformation in an algorithm.

III.5.2 Composite Block Encodings from Matrix Arithmetic

The full power of block encodings extends not merely to constructing a matrix within a quantum algorithm but also to performing a broad range of arithmetic operations, such as products and linear combinations, on the encoded matrices. Such arithmetic can be used, for example, to construct a Taylor series of 1/A1/A in a quantum linear solver [65] or a Jacobi-Anger expansion of sin⁡(A​t)\sin(At) in Hamiltonian simulation [61].

Qualtran provides a library of composite block encodings to perform arithmetic operations over the primitive forms of block encoding above; we summarize them in Table 3. Given a sequence of block encodings {ℬ⁡[Ai]}i\{\mathcal{B}[A_{i}]\}_{i}, Qualtran provides the TensorProduct bloq to compute ℬ⁡[⨂iAi]\mathcal{B}[\bigotimes_{i}A_{i}] and Product to compute ℬ⁡[∏iAi]\mathcal{B}[\prod_{i}A_{i}]. It provides the bloqs Phase to compute ℬ⁡[exp⁡(i​ϕ)​A1]\mathcal{B}[\exp{i\phi}A_{1}] and LinearCombination to compute ℬ⁡[∑iλi​Ai]\mathcal{B}[\sum_{i}\lambda_{i}A_{i}] given appropriate 0≤ϕ<2​π0\leq\phi<2\pi or λi∈ℝ\lambda_{i}\in\mathbb{R} respectively [72].

In Fig. 6(b), we illustrate how a developer uses Qualtran’s block encoding library to perform arithmetic on the encoded matrices. Specifically, the example constructs a block encoding of the Chebyshev polynomial T2​(A)=2​A2−IT_{2}(A)=2A^{2}-I given a block encoding of AA. It does so by invoking the Unitary bloq to block-encode II, invoking the Product bloq on AA with itself, and then invoking the LinearCombination bloq to produce the final polynomial. In Fig. 6(c), we visualize the more complex underlying sequence of bloq operations to which the high-level programs in Figs. 6(a) and 6(b) compile.

III.5.3 Optimizing and Analyzing Block Encodings

Qualtran also provides more optimized implementations for certain forms of arithmetic with appropriate structure. One example is the ChebyshevPolynomial bloq, described in Section IV.1, that can implement the transformation of Fig. 6(b) using fewer ancillas and gates. The user can further improve the efficiency of arithmetic by rewriting its algebraic structure. For example, Qualtran provides a function collect_like_terms to flatten nested linear combinations and thereby save qubits and gates.

To the researcher, one useful feature is that Qualtran can automatically analyze the properties—normalization factor α\alpha, ancilla overhead aa, and precision ϵ\epsilon—that determine the efficiency of a block encoding and in turn the resource consumption of the quantum algorithm. Under the hood, Qualtran leverages its support for symbolics to automatically derive values for these parameters from the constituents of a composite block encoding, e.g. the terms being added in a LinearCombination.

III.6 Quantum Signal Processing

Quantum Signal Processing (QSP) is a quantum algorithmic primitive to which many standard quantum algorithms can be reduced. Given a unitary UU and a polynomial PP, QSP implements a block-encoding (Section III.5) of P⁡(U)P(U). QSP is a building block for Quantum Singular Value Transformation (QSVT) [72], which transforms singular values of a block-encoded matrix. QSVT has been used to design algorithms for many problems, including quantum linear systems [70] and Hamiltonian simulation [61]. See Refs. [74, 72] for an exposition.

Qualtran provides a GeneralizedQSP bloq [75] which allows applying a complex polynomial PP to obtain a block-encoding of P⁡(U)P(U). The bloq is parameterized by a pair of complex polynomials P,QP,Q, and a unitary bloq UU, and implements the unitary

𝖦𝖰𝖲𝖯P,Q​(U)=[P⁡(U)⋅Q⁡(U)⋅]\mathsf{GQSP}_{P,Q}(U)=\begin{bmatrix}P(U)&\cdot~\\ Q(U)&\cdot~\end{bmatrix}

The polynomial PP above should satisfy |P⁡(ei​θ)|≤1\absolutevalue{P(e^{i\theta})}\leq 1 for all θ∈[0,2​π)\theta\in[0,2\pi). For a degree dd polynomial PP, the bloq uses dd calls to controlled-UU, along with d+1d+1 arbitrary single qubit rotations.

While the polynomial transformation PP is usually defined by the algorithmic designer, it can be challenging to compute the complementary polynomial QQ. QQ should be constructed such that

|P⁡(ei​θ)|2+|Q⁡(ei​θ)|2=1for all θ∈[0,2​π).\absolutevalue{P(e^{i\theta})}^{2}+\absolutevalue{Q(e^{i\theta})}^{2}=1\quad\quad\text{for all $\theta\in[0,2\pi)$.}

Qualtran implements three methods to compute the complementary polynomial QQ provided an input PP:

  1. 1.

    qsp_complementary_polynomial: By factorizing PP [75, Theorem 4] (default).

  2. 2.

    fast_complementary_polynomial: Convex optimization [75, Theorem 4].

  3. 3.

    fft_complementary_polynomial: A fast Fourier transform-based method [76, Algorithm 2].

Figure 7 shows an example GQSP circuit implementing the polynomial P⁡(x)=(x2+1)/2P(x)=(x^{2}+1)/2 using Algorithm 1 of Ref. [75].

III.7 Quantum Phase Estimation

In this section, we detail Qualtran’s support for a variety of phase estimation bloqs, primarily distinguished by their use of different window functions to minimize phase measurement uncertainty - quantified by metrics like probability of error outside a confidence interval and Holevo variance. We begin with a concise mathematical overview essential for describing the implemented bloqs, followed by their applications in quantum metrology and simulation. A summary of supported bloqs can be found in Table 4.

Given a unitary UU with an eigenvector |ψ⟩\ket{\psi} and eigenvalue e2​π​i​ϕe^{2\pi i\phi}, such that U​|ψ⟩=e2​π​i​ϕ​|ψ⟩U\ket{\psi}=e^{2\pi i\phi}\ket{\psi}, Quantum Phase Estimation (QPE) aims to output an estimate of ϕ\phi - the eigenphase corresponding to |ψ⟩\ket{\psi} [77, 78, 45]. When (a) the eigenstate state |ψ⟩\ket{\psi} is exactly prepared and given as an input and (b) the eigenphase ϕ\phi is a dyadic rational (i.e. it can be represented exactly with a finite number of bits - mm), then the action of QPE can be described as

QPE​|ψ⟩​|0⟩m→|ψ⟩​|ϕ⟩\text{QPE}\ket{\psi}\ket{0}^{m}\rightarrow\ket{\psi}\ket{\phi}

In practice, however, both the assumptions (a) and (b) stated above are hard to achieve. In a more general setting, given an input unitary UU with an eigendecomposition U=∑je2​π​i​ϕj​|ψj⟩​⟨ψj|U=\sum_{j}e^{2\pi i\phi_{j}}\ket{\psi_j}\bra{\psi_j}, an input initial state |Ψ⟩=∑jγj​|ψj⟩\ket{\Psi}=\sum_{j}\gamma_{j}\ket{\psi_j} and an auxiliary control register |0⟩m\ket{0}^{m}, QPE allows us to sample from the eigenspectrum of UU by applying the map

QPE​|Ψ⟩​|0⟩m→∑j∑kγj​τ​(j,k)​|ψj⟩​|ϕk⟩~\text{QPE}\ket{\Psi}\ket{0}^{m}\rightarrow\sum_{j}\sum_{k}\gamma_{j}\tau(j,k)\ket{\psi_j}\tilde{\ket{\phi_k}} (9)

where τ⁡(x,y)\tau(x,y) is a kernel function and ϕj~\tilde{\phi_{j}} is an mm-bit approximation to the desired phase ϕj\phi_{j}. If ∀j\forall_{j}, ϕj\phi_{j} can be represented exactly using mm bits then τ⁡(x,y)=δx,y\tau(x,y)=\delta_{x,y} such that QPE​|Ψ⟩​|0⟩m→∑jγj​|ψj⟩​|ϕj⟩\text{QPE}\ket{\Psi}\ket{0}^{m}\rightarrow\sum_{j}\gamma_{j}\ket{\psi_j}\ket{\phi_j}.

From Equation 9, one can see that on measuring the mm-bit auxiliary control register in the computational basis, the probability of getting a phase |ϕk⟩~\tilde{\ket{\phi_k}} can be written as

Pr[ϕ^=ϕk~]=∑j|γj|2|τ⁡(j,k)|2\Pr[\hat{\phi}=\tilde{\phi_{k}}]=\sum_{j}\absolutevalue{\gamma_{j}}^{2}\absolutevalue{\tau(j, k)}^{2} (10)

Here ϕ^\hat{\phi} is a random variable that corresponds to the phase estimate, and can be decomposed as

ϕ^=ϕ+Δ​ϕ\hat{\phi}=\phi+\Delta\phi (11)

where ϕ\phi is a random variable satisfying Pr[ϕ=ϕj]=|γj|2\Pr[\phi=\phi_{j}]=\absolutevalue{\gamma_j}^{2} and Δ​ϕ\Delta\phi is a random variable satisfying conditional distribution Pr⁡[Δ​ϕ=ϕk^−ϕk|ϕk]=|τ⁡(j,k)|2\Pr[\Delta\phi=\hat{\phi_{k}}-\phi_{k}|\phi_{k}]=\absolutevalue{\tau(j, k)}^{2}. Here ϕ\phi represents the likelihood of projecting the initial state |Ψ⟩\ket{\Psi} into the desired eigenstate |ψj⟩\ket{\psi_j}, which depends solely on the initial overlap γj\gamma_{j}, and Δ​ϕ\Delta\phi represents a phase error introduced due to spectral leakage [79, 80], a phenomenon where probability spreads across multiple peaks due to misalignment between the true phase ϕj\phi_{j} and the discrete values ϕk~\tilde{\phi_{k}} used to approximate ϕj\phi_{j} using a finite number of bits mm.

Window functions are tools borrowed from classical signal processing that can be used to smooth out the sharp transitions at the edges of a probability distribution and concentrate probability mass around the true phase [81]. In QPE, the state preparation unitary used to construct an initial state on the auxiliary control register of size mm, is referred to as a window state. In Qualtran, QPEWindowStateBase class defines an interface for bloqs that can be used to prepare window states for QPE.

TextbookQPE bloq in Qualtran accepts any unitary bloq UU, an instance of QPEWindowStateBase for preparing an initial window state on the control register of bitsize mm and applies mm controlled unitaries, C-U2i\text{C-U}^{2^{i}} in the ii’th step, followed by an inverse QFT.

QubitizationQPE bloq in Qualtran accepts an instance of QubitizationWalkOperator WW [61], an instance of QPEWindowStateBase for preparing an initial window state on the control register of bitsize mm, and implements the optimization from Figure 2 of Babbush et al. [9] to double the phase difference and apply powers of controlled walk operator by only controlling the reflection operator.

In Qualtran, for both the QPE bloqs desribed above, the cost of QPE on mm control qubits is reported as a sum of costs for

  1. 1.

    CtrlStatePrep: Cost to prepare the window state on mm control qubits, typically scales as 𝒪⁡(m)\mathcal{O}(m). For the textbook version of QPE [45], the window state is a Rectangular window - prepared by simply applying a Hadamard gate on all mm control qubits.

  2. 2.

    Controlled-U’s: There are two cases:

    • •

      If the unitary is fast forwardable; i.e. cost of C-Un\text{C-U}^{n} scales sublinearly with nn, the cost of this step is at least m×cost(C-U)m\times\text{cost(C-U)}

    • •

      If the unitary is not fast forwardable; i.e. cost of C-Un\text{C-U}^{n} is n×cost(C-U)n\times\text{cost(C-U)}, the cost of this step is 2m×cost(C-U)2^{m}\times\text{cost(C-U)}.

  3. 3.

    QFT†\text{QFT}^{\dagger}: The textbook version of inverse QFT uses 𝒪⁡(m2)\mathcal{O}(m^{2}) rotations [45] but this can be improved to 𝒪⁡(m​log⁡(m))\mathcal{O}(m\log{m}) using approximate QFT constructions [82, 83].

From the enumeration above one can see that in general, when the unitary UU is not fast forwardable, the number of queries made by the Quantum Phase Estimation (QPE) procedure to the controlled unitary C-U scales exponentially with the number of control qubits mm. Qualtran provides bloqs to prepare a variety of different initial window states, summarized in Table 4, which can be used to determine the minimum of number of control qubits mm required to keep the uncertainty in the measured phase below a certain threshold ϵ\epsilon.

Below, we describe the two most commonly used measures of uncertainty in the estimated phase and corresponding Qualtran bloqs to prepare window states which are optimal for minimizing the uncertainty.

III.7.1 Minimizing Probability of Error Outside a Confidence Interval

One way to characterize the uncertainty Δ​ϕ\Delta\phi is to bound the probability with which the measured phase ϕ~\tilde{\phi} is outside of a confidence interval around the true phase ϕ\phi of half-width ϵ\epsilon, defined as [ϕ−ϵ,ϕ+ϵ][\phi-\epsilon,\phi+\epsilon]. This version is also known as high-confidence QPE

Pr[Δϕ>ϵ]≤δ\Pr\left[\Delta\phi>\epsilon\right]\leq\delta

It is known that a phase estimation protocol with precision ϵ\epsilon and error probability δ\delta has cost Ω⁡(1ϵ​log⁡(1δ))\Omega(\frac{1}{\epsilon}\log{\frac{1}{\delta}})[91] and this can be achieved by using Kaiser window based control states [89, 79] or Discrete Prolate Spheroidal Sequence (DPSS) [92, 93, 90] based control states. In Qualtran, the KaiserWindowState bloq can be used to initialize the control register in the Kaiser window state, given a specific choice of parameter α\alpha, and uses bloqs for arbitrary state preparation described in Section III.4.

Minimizing the probability of error outside a confidence interval is a useful measure of uncertainty in applications where

  • •

    The relationship between the desired quantity and estimated phase is nonlinear and the application is highly sensitive to errors outside the confidence interval. For example - amplitude estimation in [89], variable time amplitude amplification in [94] or ground state energy estimation by taking minimum of sampled values.

  • •

    When the choice of parameter δ\delta is well motivated, the high confidence version leads to optimal constant factors.

III.7.2 Minimizing Holevo Variance

The Holevo variance, defined as VH=⟨cos⁡(Δ​ϕ)⟩−2−1V_{H}=\langle\cos{\Delta\phi}\rangle^{-2}-1, is a convenient measure of variance for phase because it enables simple analytic results and is close to the mean-square error for narrowly peaked distributions [95, 96]. Specifically, it can be shown [9, 97] that there exists a phase estimation protocol which uses mm control qubits and 2m2^{m} applications of Controlled-U to yield an estimate of the phase ϕ~\tilde{\phi} such that

𝔼⁡(Δ​ϕ)=0​ and ​VH​(Δ​ϕ)=tan2⁡(π2m+1)≈(π2m)2\mathbb{E}(\Delta\phi)=0\text{ and }V_{H}(\Delta\phi)=\tan^{2}\left({\frac{\pi}{2^{m}+1}}\right)\approx\left(\frac{\pi}{2^{m}}\right)^{2}

In Qualtran, LPResourceState bloq can be used to initialize the control register in Sine state, which are optimal control states [86] to minimize the Holevo variance, using a single round of amplitude amplification via the procedure described in [9].

Holevo variance is a useful measure of uncertainty in applications where

  • •

    The estimated phase is treated as a continuous quantity and the magnitude of the error is also important. For example in quantum metrology [96].

  • •

    The relationship between the desired quantity and estimated phase is linear, so one can take advantage of variance bounds on the estimated phase to obtain variance bounds on the desired quantity. For example - finite difference estimation of forces from [15].

  • •

    The variance version is easy to get rough resource estimates since its parameter free. The confidence interval version requires a choice of probability outside the confidence interval δ\delta. If the precise value for choosing δ\delta is not well motivated, optimal variance-minimizing phase estimation version is more convenient to use [9].

IV Case Study 1: Hamiltonian Simulation

Hamiltonian simulation implements a unitary e−i​H​te^{-iHt} given access to a Hamiltonian HH [61]. This case study discusses two methods of simulating block-encoded hamiltonians: by constructing block-encodings of cos⁡H\cos H and sin⁡H\sin H using Chebyshev polynomials, and by using GQSP to directly implement approximations for e−i​H​te^{-iHt}. Both these methods use qubitization to convert the input block-encoding of HH into a special block-encoding with useful properties. We first describe qubitization, and then proceed to show Qualtran implementations of the two hamiltonian simulation techniques stated above.

IV.1 Qubitization

Qubitization [61] is a technique to transform an arbitrary block encoding ℬ⁡[A]\mathcal{B}[A], to an equivalent block encoding 𝒲⁡[A]\mathcal{W}[A] whose eigenvalues correspond to the eigenvalues of AA. This enables performing operations on the block encoding 𝒲⁡[A]\mathcal{W}[A] to transform the eigenvalues of AA. This operator 𝒲⁡[A]\mathcal{W}[A] is usually called a qubitized quantum walk operator. More generally, qubitization can be combined with QSP/GQSP (Section III.6) to implement arbitrary polynomials of block-encoded matrices, called the Quantum Singular Value Transformation [72]. See Ref. [98], Sec. 10.4 for a detailed pedagogical exposition.

Qualtran provides QubitizationWalkOperator that implements 𝒲⁡[A]\mathcal{W}[A] given a BlockEncoding ℬ⁡[A]\mathcal{B}[A]. It assumes that the input block-encoding ℬ⁡[A]\mathcal{B}[A] is a reflection (i.e. ℬ​[A]2=I\mathcal{B}[A]^{2}=I), and implements 𝒲⁡[A]\mathcal{W}[A] using one call to ℬ⁡[A]\mathcal{B}[A] [61, Corollary 9]. Figure 8 shows an example qubitized walk operator for the Hubbard Hamiltonian [9, Sec. 5], using the block-encoding of the Hubbard model.

IV.2 Hamiltonian simulation using Chebyshev Polynomials

The ChebyshevPolynomial bloq uses qubitization to efficiently compute ℬ​[Tj​(A/α)]\mathcal{B}[T_{j}(A/\alpha)], where Tj​(x)T_{j}(x) is the jj-th Chebyshev polynomial of the first kind. This uses jj calls to the corresponding walk operator 𝒲⁡[A]\mathcal{W}[A].

The ScaledChebyshevPolynomial bloq implements an appropriately scaled ℬ​[Tj​(A)]\mathcal{B}[T_{j}(A)], by combining the above ChebyshevPolynomial with a LinearCombination.

Using the above bloqs, Fig. 9 shows an implementation of Hamiltonian simulation of a block-encoded HH by computing the block-encoding of cos⁡(H​t)\cos(Ht) and sin⁡(H​t)\sin(Ht) using Chebyshev polynomials.

IV.3 Hamiltonian Simulation using GQSP

Low and Chuang [61] describe an efficient Hamiltionian simulation by combining quantum signal processing (QSP) with qubitization. Qualtran provides the HamiltonianSimulationByGQSP bloq, which takes in a BlockEncoding ℬ⁡[H]\mathcal{B}[H] which is an (α,a,0)(\alpha,a,0)-block-encoding of HH, a time parameter tt, and a precision ϵ\epsilon and implements a (1,a+1,ϵ)(1,a+1,\epsilon)-block-encoding of e−i​H​te^{-iHt}. It does this by computing a GQSP polynomial PP that is ϵ\epsilon-close to f⁡(ei​θ)=e−i​α​t​cos⁡(θ)f(e^{i\theta})=e^{-i\alpha t\cos(\theta)}, using the Jacobi-Anger expansion. This GQSP bloq is applied to the qubitized walk operator of the input block-encoding. The degree of this polynomial approximation scales as

𝒪⁡(α​t+log⁡(1/ϵ)log⁡log⁡(1/ϵ))\order{\alpha t + \frac{\log(1/\epsilon)}{\log\log(1/\epsilon)}}

The polynomial approximations can be found in qualtran.linalg.polynomial. Figure 10 shows an example snippet for simulating the 2D Hubbard Hamiltonian [9, Sec. 5] using HamiltonianSimulationByGQSP.

V Case Study 2: Computing Ground States in Quantum Chemistry

Simulating chemical systems is one of the most cited use cases of fault tolerant quantum computers. In particular, computing the ground state or the low lying excited states of challenging molecules is seen as a good task for quantum phase estimation. Over the years, the cost of performing phase estimation has reduced by 6 orders of magnitude, from 101610^{16} to 101010^{10} Toffoli gates [17]. Most of these improvements have been driven by the adoption of modern factorizations [56, 13, 17] of the two electron integrals necessary to specify the Hamiltonian, and also through the use of different representations (i.e. first quantization [12].)

These algorithms can be built up from the extensive library of primitives that qualtran provides (see Section III), thus avoiding the toil of parsing 100 page papers. Qualtran provides block encodings for all four variants of the second quantized Hamiltonian (sparse, single-factorized, double-factorized, and tensor hypercontraction (THC)), as well as for the first quantized algorithm with and without a quantum projectile [12, 10]. Many of these algorithms are implemented in a top down fashion, without being compiled all the way down to primitive gates, while some (THC, and the sparse representation) have more detailed implementations.

V.1 Resource Estimation and Algorithm Analysis

A common task for researchers is computing the costs for performing phase estimation for a specific molecule of interest. Traditionally this has been done by manually enumerating costs in standalone notebooks which may or may not be published, or using open source tools like OpenFermion. While OpenFermion does provide tools for resource estimation of second quantized hamiltonians, the implemention is simply a hardcoded list of formulae with no real way to modify the values or attribute individual costs do different quantum subroutines or primitives. Qualtran, in contrast, builds up the algorithms in a structured way, allowing for cost analysis along the call graph of the algorithm as well as enabling algorithm modification and the reuse of subcomponents. Fig. 11(a) demonstrates how Qualtran provides an intuitive way to compute resource estimates and categorize the costs for a particular form of chemical Hamiltonian.

Fig. 11(b) shows the utility of writing algorithms in a structured way, as qualtran can easily classify costs by the type of primitive. Finally, Table 5 shows that the block encoding costs are consistent with reported literature values (recomputed with OpenFermion for comparison) for the FeMoco model system.

Qualtran also provides block encodings for the first quantized representation [12], which are not available in OpenFermion. Again, the structured way of writing algorithms in qualtran allows for additional insight into the algorithms as shown in Fig. 12, which demonstrates that in this algorithm SELECT (dominated by controlled swaps) is the dominant cost as the number of electrons (η\eta) grows.

V.2 Symbolic Analysis

Quantum algorithms typically only allow us to estimate properties to within some additive error ϵ\epsilon, which often is a combination of different sources of errors arising from different parts of the algorithm. An example of this is Trotterized phase estimation which introduces three sources of controllable error: 1) the Suzuki-Trotter error ΔT​S\Delta_{TS}, 2) the phase estimation error ΔP​E\Delta_{PE}, and, 3) the rotation synthesis error ΔH​T\Delta_{HT} [100, 101]. A common task is to optimize the costs such that ϵ≤ΔT​S+ΔH​T+ΔP​E\epsilon\leq\Delta_{TS}+\Delta_{HT}+\Delta_{PE}. The rotation synthesis cost is a parameter of all rotation bloqs in qualtran, while the trotter error and phase estimation error are incorporated in higher level TrotterizedUnitary, and PhaseEstimation bloqs. By propagating these symbolic costs, Qualtran can automatically produce mathematical expressions for the algorithm’s cost. Fig. 13 provides a code-snippet for generating the Trotterized phase estimation costs for the 2D Hubbard model [100, 101] while Eq. 12 is the resulting output.

Tcost=0.76​π​(ΔT​Sξ)−1p​((2​L2+6​⌊L22⌋)​⌈1.149​log2⁡(1.0​NR​(ΔT​Sξ)−1pΔH​T)+9.2⌉+24​⌊L22⌋)ΔP​ET_{\mathrm{cost}}=\frac{0.76\pi\left(\frac{\Delta_{TS}}{\xi}\right)^{-\frac{1}{p}}\left(\left(2L^{2}+6\left\lfloor{\frac{L^{2}}{2}}\right\rfloor\right)\left\lceil{1.149\operatorname{log}_{2}{\left(\frac{1.0N_{R}\left(\frac{\Delta_{TS}}{\xi}\right)^{-\frac{1}{p}}}{\Delta_{HT}}\right)}+9.2}\right\rceil+24\left\lfloor{\frac{L^{2}}{2}}\right\rfloor\right)}{\Delta_{PE}} (12)

Here, NRN_{R} is the number of single qubit rotations in a single Trotter step which depends on the order of the Trotter expansion pp. The user can numerically optimize this expression (see Fig. 14) to arrive at the lowest cost algorithm subject to the constraint on ϵ\epsilon.

VI Case Study 3: Cryptography

One of the earliest pieces of evidence for the power of quantum computation was Shor’s introduction of algorithms for factoring and the discrete logarithm [2]. With sufficiently powerful hardware, these algorithms could be used to break commonly used cryptosystems including RSA and elliptic curve cryptography (ECC). As such, it is particularly essential to accurately estimate the quantum resource requirements and costs. These estimates can already impact contemporary decisions about the urgency of the move to post-quantum cryptography e.g. for data that remains sensitive as long as the timeframes under consideration.

Given the impact of these algorithms, a number of compilation and resource estimation studies have been applied to optimizing the primitives used for factoring and breaking RSA and ECC [102, 103, 104, 105, 106, 107, 108, 109]. Some studies [105, 107] have even published explicit code in the Q# programming language with complete implementations. We summarize some of the leading constructions for RSA and ECC and show how Qualtran can be used for these algorithms. We use automated routines to highlight expensive parts of the algorithm, show how the classical simulation protocol can aid in testing of classical reversible logic, and automatically propagate symbolic costs for an important subroutine.

The setting for both RSA factoring and elliptic curve cryptography starts with a finite field. The quantum algorithm uses phase estimation of the field’s group multiplication operation to extract the hidden property of interest. The field and group operation differ between the two schemes, but the group operation is always a classical operation that we must execute on a quantum superposition of inputs. Optimization of these constructions, therefore, need not be performed by experts in quantum information. The structure and organization of a library such as Qualtran can help solicit contributions from classical computer scientists as well as traditional quantum algorithms researchers.
